evidence_text: Fernbank Logistics grew its workforce to 1,200 people this year, adding warehouse and driver roles across every region.

metadata.source_note: 'Grew its workforce to 1,200 people' is a legitimate paraphrase of 'headcount rose to 1,200 employees' — same metric under a different noun, operator entailed from 'grew', unit equivalent (people ~ employees). Tests whether annotators correctly treat this as supported rather than over-applying the strict-metric rule meant for genuinely different metrics like 'revenue' vs 'gross revenue'.

claim_text: Ridgeline Analytics served roughly two hundred enterprise customers as of last quarter.
evidence_text: Ridgeline Analytics closed out the quarter serving one hundred and ninety-eight enterprise accounts, per its board deck.

metadata.source_note: Numbers are spelled out in words on both sides and phrased approximately ('roughly two hundred' vs 'one hundred and ninety-eight'), so no deterministic substring match resolves valueUnit — it must go to judge field extraction. Built specifically to exercise the blind-answering step: the judge should extract '198 enterprise accounts' from the evidence WITHOUT being shown the claim's '200' first, so the deterministic comparator (not the judge) decides whether 198 counts as matching or conflicting with a claim that says 'roughly two hundred'. Annotators should record what they believe the correct extracted evidence value is, independent of the claim, exactly as the judge is meant to.

claim_text: Harvest Commons, a food-security nonprofit, kept administrative overhead below 10% last year.
evidence_text: Harvest Commons' audited financials show management and general expenses at 9.2% of total functional expenses for the year, per its Form 990. Fundraising expenses, reported separately at 6.1%, are not included in that figure.

metadata.source_note: Genuinely hard: 'administrative overhead' is a colloquial term with no single standard accounting definition. The evidence gives 'management and general expenses' (9.2%), which nonprofit-accounting convention usually treats as the 'administrative' component, but a stricter reader could argue fundraising costs should also count toward 'overhead' (would push the number to 15.3%, breaking the claim). Deliberately included to stress-test the annotator guide's metric-identity rule on a real-world ambiguous term rather than a clean field-name mismatch — expect disagreement here, which is the point.

claim_text: Ashcombe College's graduation rate improved to 85% for the class of 2024.
evidence_text: Ashcombe College's six-year graduation rate for the cohort that entered in fall 2018 (the class of 2024) reached 85%, up two points from the prior cohort, the registrar's office reported.

metadata.source_note: Hard call on metric identity: the claim just says 'graduation rate' but the only evidence available is specifically the federal six-year graduation-rate measure. A reader could treat 'six-year graduation rate' as the same metric as an unqualified 'graduation rate' for this cohort label (since 'class of 2024' inherently implies the six-year cohort convention in US higher-ed reporting), or could treat the unqualified claim as ambiguous between a four-year and six-year measure and therefore not clearly matched. Included to test how annotators handle a claim whose metric is under-specified relative to a precisely-defined evidence figure.
